questions.prompt: What is an equilibrium position?
questions.answer: The position where the mass can rest.
rubric: Identify the resting position.

questions.prompt: A moving mass reaches equilibrium. Why can it continue past that point?
questions.answer: Its inertia keeps it moving. After it passes equilibrium, the spring acts back toward equilibrium from the other side.
rubric: Explain that inertia carries the mass past equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Describe the difference between longitudinal and transverse motion.
questions.answer: Longitudinal motion runs along the spring line; transverse motion runs across it.
rubric: Distinguish motion along the line from motion across it.

questions.prompt: Why do the two directions of motion have the same frequency in the example?
questions.answer: Their moving masses and total restoring stiffnesses are matched. Direction alone does not determine how fast they repeat.
rubric: Connect the matched rate with matched mass and restoring stiffness.

questions.prompt: What happens to frequency when mass increases and stiffness stays the same?
questions.answer: Frequency falls.
rubric: Give a decrease in frequency.

questions.prompt: Why does greater stiffness make the same mass oscillate faster?
questions.answer: The same displacement produces a stronger restoring force. It changes the mass’s movement more quickly, so each cycle takes less time.
rubric: Connect a stronger restoring force with a quicker cycle.

questions.prompt: Why does making a transverse spring harder to stretch not automatically establish a higher transverse restoring force?
questions.answer: The restoring force across the spring line depends on the tension and arrangement of its segments. Hardness to stretch along the spring is not by itself the same property.
rubric: Distinguish axial stretch stiffness from the restoring action across the line.

questions.prompt: What is a normal mode?
questions.answer: A coordinated movement pattern in which the connected masses keep a particular relationship to one another while repeating at one frequency.
rubric: Identify a repeating coordinated pattern with a particular relationship between the parts.

questions.prompt: Which mode makes the two masses move together?
questions.answer: Mode 1.
rubric: Identify Mode 1.

questions.prompt: Why is the opposite-moving mode faster in the two-mass chain?
questions.answer: The masses stretch and compress their middle connection more strongly when they move against each other. This adds restoring action and makes the pattern repeat faster.
rubric: Connect opposite movement with stronger changes in the middle connection.
Connect restoring action with higher frequency.

questions.prompt: What does superposition mean in the two-mass example?
questions.answer: At each mass, the movements contributed by the modes add. Contributions in the same direction reinforce one another, while opposite contributions partly cancel.
rubric: Explain adding the contributions at the same mass.

questions.prompt: In Mode 1 of the three-mass chain, do all masses move the same distance? Explain.
questions.answer: No. They move in the same direction together, but the middle mass moves farther and the two outer masses move equal, smaller distances.
rubric: Distinguish sharing direction from moving equal distances.

questions.prompt: In Mode 2 of the three-mass chain, what does the middle mass do?
questions.answer: It stays at equilibrium.
rubric: Identify the stationary middle mass.

questions.prompt: Describe Mode 3 of the three-mass chain.
questions.answer: The outer masses move together while the middle mass moves against them.
rubric: Identify the middle mass moving opposite to the outer two.

questions.prompt: In the three-mass chain, why can the middle mass move in a mixture even though it is still in Mode 2?
questions.answer: Modes 1 and 3 contribute movement at the middle mass. Being still in Mode 2 does not fix that mass in every possible pattern.
rubric: Connect the movement with contributions from other modes.

questions.prompt: How many independent modes does a five-mass chain have in the displayed direction?
questions.answer: Five.
rubric: Give five modes.

questions.prompt: What changes across higher modes of the same chain if the masses and connections are unchanged?
questions.answer: There are more reversals along the chain, with different regions moving opposite ways. These patterns have higher frequencies.
rubric: Identify more opposite-moving regions and higher frequencies.

questions.prompt: Does having three modes mean that their frequencies must be one, two, and three times the lowest frequency?
questions.answer: No. The frequencies of a chain of separate masses generally do not have that exact whole-number spacing.
rubric: Distinguish number of modes from harmonic frequency spacing.

questions.prompt: What is a node on the fixed–fixed string?
questions.answer: A position that remains at zero displacement throughout that mode’s motion.
rubric: Identify a position that stays still.

questions.prompt: How many half-waves fit the fixed–fixed string in Mode 3?
questions.answer: Three half-waves.
rubric: Give three half-waves.

questions.prompt: What do the spectrum’s horizontal axis and vertical peak heights represent?
questions.answer: The horizontal axis gives frequency in hertz. Peak height gives the amplitude of each frequency component in the measured movement.
rubric: Identify frequency horizontally and amplitude vertically.

questions.prompt: What does the membrane label (2,2) mean?
questions.answer: The pattern divides into two moving regions along each surface direction, making four regions.
rubric: Identify the two-by-two division.

questions.prompt: Why does the membrane’s evenly spaced spectrum not show that all natural membranes have harmonic frequencies?
questions.answer: The frequencies were assigned for this illustration. They were not calculated natural frequencies of the rectangular membrane.
rubric: Distinguish assigned demonstration frequencies from natural frequencies.

questions.prompt: What experiment could test the predicted harmonic structure of vocal-fold vibration?
questions.answer: Record actual laryngeal vibration and examine its spectrum. Compare the spacing between the peaks with the predicted equal spacing.
rubric: Specify a laryngeal vibration measurement.
Compare its spectral spacing with the prediction.

questions.prompt: Why are even harmonics absent from the ideal fixed–free example?
questions.answer: The pattern must have a node at the fixed end and an antinode at the free end. Odd numbers of quarter-waves fit those conditions; an even number would put a node at the free end.
rubric: Connect odd quarter-waves with the different endpoint conditions.
